transfer.scenario: A reader learns her mortgage application was declined by her bank's automated affordability model before any human reviewed it.
transfer.question: Do the profile's three questions transfer usefully to this unseen automated decision without requiring facts we don't have?
transfer.answer: Yes, as questions. She can ask the bank: What is this model trying to achieve — minimizing default risk, and by what measure? What might it miss — income it wasn't shown, context a form can't capture, or circumstances it may not weigh? Who carries the consequence if it is wrong — me, and is there a human appeal route? None of these requires asserting what the model actually optimizes, what inputs it used, or why it declined her; they are inquiries she can put to the responsible institution.
transfer.assessment: The three questions transfer cleanly: they generate concrete, answerable inquiries about an unseen consequential system while keeping the reader in the questioner's seat. I did not assert the unseen system's objective, inputs, omissions or causal effect as established fact — each is framed as something to ask or a possibility to check. This confirms the About's reader consequence is a real capability, not decorative.

issues.finding: The Penguin liver-transplant framing ('Who would you want in charge of organ allocation?') is compressed to 'who should decide who receives a life-saving liver', a slight shift from allocation-oversight to recipient-selection. The publisher copy's queue-position framing keeps this within fair paraphrase, so it is not material, but a stricter rendering would say 'who should be in charge of allocating a life-saving liver'.
issues.artifactExcerpt: who should decide who receives a life-saving liver

summary: Candidate PASS; incumbent control REJECT. I read the complete candidate text first, then both complete primary sources. The successor About replaces a title-only biography with a compact 97-word treatment that (1) states a distinctive contribution anchored to the Leelavati citation's own language, (2) gives one concrete sourced example — Hello World's sentencing and liver-allocation questions, correctly attributed to Penguin publisher copy with its limitation respected, (3) hands the reader three portable questions that independently transfer to an unseen automated decision (tested on a mortgage-decline scenario, questions-only), and (4) keeps Hello World plus seven byte-identical links as entry points. All locked fields (id, name, role, lesson, image, links, freshness) are preserved per the change proof. Voice is third-person and factual with explicit attribution; no award-list substitution, jargon, founder voice or inspirational ending — it ends on usable questions. One minor issue only: the liver question compresses 'in charge of organ allocation' to 'who receives a life-saving liver', a fair but slightly loose paraphrase; not material. Zero material issues, so PASS stands. The incumbent negative control receives its own independent REJECT: a bare title supplies none of the four required elements.
